title: The teachers, closed
hookLine: from Nagarjuna to the village grandmother

lines: AJAHN CHAH. DIPA MA. MAHA GHOSANANDA.
cards: Lay them out like photographs on a long table. Nagarjuna, arguing that nothing stands on its own. Asanga, bending over a wounded dog.
Shantideva, the monk the others thought was lazy, standing up to recite. Atisha keeping his bad-tempered cook. Milarepa hauling stones for towers he was told to tear down.
Machig Labdron offering her body to fear. Dogen just sitting. Hakuin saying is that so.
Ryokan wishing he could give a thief the moon. The nun Chiyono and her broken bucket. Ajahn Chah in the forest, Dipa Ma in her small apartment, Maha Ghosananda walking for peace.

teach.b: Here's what's strange: the Buddha seemed to see this long run of teachers coming, and to warn against leaning on any one of them too hard.
In the discourse on his final passing, Ananda is worried about what happens when the Buddha is gone. The answer, in T. W.
Rhys Davids' translation: "be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves."
Just before that, he tells Ananda he has no closed fist of a teacher, nothing kept back for a chosen few.
And near the end, as this path heard a few days ago, he says the teaching and the discipline will be their teacher after he is gone. So in the Buddha's own words, the real teacher is the teaching.

teach.h: THEY CARRIED IT FOR A STRETCH.
teach.b: Every name on that table carried it for a stretch and handed it on. Nagarjuna's logic and the grandmother's lamp-lighting aren't competing; they're two people holding the same lamp at different points on the road.
Some were brilliant, some wild, some quiet. Some were saints in their tradition's eyes, and this block also made room for teachers who failed. None of them is the point.

teach.h: A GOOD TEACHER POINTS PAST THEMSELVES.
teach.b: The Pali word for a teacher is acariya, and in this light a good acariya points past themselves, toward the teaching. Whoever practices today is somewhere on that table, holding the lamp for a while.

how: Buddhists honor their teachers in chants of lineage, in portraits on altars and in memorial days, while the texts point to the teaching itself as the teacher after the Buddha.

o: the founders of each Buddhist school
monks who were declared to be saints
those who carried the teaching for a while

p: what the Buddha says he doesn't have

s: the Buddha kept secret teachings back for a chosen few
he told Ananda he had no closed fist of a teacher, holding things back.
"be ye lamps unto yourselves" comes from the discourse on the Buddha's final passing
it's his answer to Ananda's worry about what comes next.
this block of teachers included only well-known names
it ended with unknown teachers, your own teachers and becoming one.

games.q: you're Ananda. the Buddha is old and ill, and you've comforted yourself that he'll leave final instructions for the community. what does he tell you?
o: I've saved the deepest teaching for last.
be lamps unto yourselves; be a refuge to yourselves.
choose the wisest monk to lead you.
games.why: he has held nothing back, he says, and he tells them to be lamps and a refuge to themselves, with the truth as their lamp.

practice: Choose one face from the table, a well-known name, your grandmother, the stranger who once told you the truth, and pick just one moment: a dog, a bucket, a cup of tea, a word. Let that moment sit beside you while you breathe.
If your mind wanders off, come back to it, the way you'd come back to a friend's voice in a noisy room.

wordCard.voice: The teachers. From Nagarjuna to the grandmother with no name, people who carried the teaching for a stretch, while, in the Buddha's words, the teaching itself stayed the teacher.

carryVoice: Your line: they carried it. None of them was the point; the lamp was. That's today, done.

sources.q: be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves.

sources.ref: Mahaparinibbana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 16) VI.1 (the teaching as teacher)
